questions.question: On a 4 by 4 grid P2 can always win by copying. If you wanted to take that away, what would you change?
options: Shade one corner square before starting
Let the loser go second next time
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. An odd side or a missing square breaks the copying; longer pieces change the counting; swapping who goes second only shares the advantage. Talk about which you would try, and what it would change.

title: SOS — write S or O, make SOS
parent_game: SOS, a pencil-and-paper game

credits.by: Traditional

lesson: Both players write the same letters, so anything you write can help your opponent. It shows how shared pieces create tactics of giving and avoiding.
intro: Players take turns writing an S or an O in an empty square. Make S-O-S in a line and you score and go again. Every letter you write may also set up your opponent.

steps.title: Grid
steps.body: Draw a grid of 4 by 4 squares.

steps.title: Write a letter
steps.body: Toss a coin to see who starts. On your turn, write S or O in any empty square. You may choose a different letter each turn.

steps.title: Score
steps.body: If your letter completes S-O-S in a straight line, across, down or diagonally, you score a point for each new SOS and take another turn.

steps.title: Full grid
steps.body: When every square is filled, the higher score wins. Equal scores are a draw.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='45' y='12' width='110' height='96' rx='3' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='58' y='34' font-family='IBM Plex Mono' font-size='10' fill='#2D3127'>P1  3</text><text x='58' y='54' font-family='IBM Plex Mono' font-size='10' fill='#2D3127'>P2  2</text></svg>

steps.title: Careful
steps.body: An S, an O and an empty square in a line, or two S's with an empty square between them, is a gift to your opponent.

what_to_notice: When did you write a letter only to avoid giving a gift?
Did the extra turn after scoring change the game?
How did the end feel when every square left was dangerous?

animation.narration: P1 writes S in the top-left corner.
P2 writes O next to it.
P1 writes S after it: S-O-S across the top. P1 scores and goes again.
P1 writes O in the bottom-left corner. An O in a corner can never be the middle of an SOS, so it gives nothing away.
Play goes on until all 16 squares are filled. The higher score wins.

questions.question: Which letters may you write?
options: S or O, your choice each turn
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look again at step 2.

questions.question: What happens when you complete an SOS?
options: You score a point and take another turn
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look again at step 3.

questions.question: Why was P2's O beside P1's S a mistake?
options: It left S-O with an empty square after it, so P1 could finish SOS
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look at what P1 did next.

questions.question: If you wanted fewer gifts and more planning, what would you change?
options: Give each player a fixed letter
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Dropping the extra turn makes a gift cost less; a fixed letter turns it into a different game; a bigger grid gives more safe squares for longer. Talk about which you would try, and what it would change.

title: Three Men's Morris — three in a row, then move
parent_game: Three Men's Morris, an old game related to tic-tac-toe

credits.by: Traditional
credits.rules: The board as recorded by the US National Park Service

lesson: Placing pieces, then moving them: a second phase keeps a tic-tac-toe-like game from ending in a draw. It shows phases as a design tool.
equipment: paper and a pen to draw the board
3 coins or pebbles each, of two kinds
intro: Like tic-tac-toe, but with only three pieces each. Once all six are down you slide pieces along the lines, so the game does not stop with a full board.

steps.title: Board
steps.body: Draw a square with nine points: the four corners, the middle of each side and the centre. Join them with lines across, down, and through the centre along both diagonals.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'><rect x='60' y='15' width='80' height='90' fill='none'/><line x1='100' y1='15' x2='100' y2='105'/><line x1='60' y1='60' x2='140' y2='60'/><line x1='60' y1='15' x2='140' y2='105'/><line x1='140' y1='15' x2='60' y2='105'/></g><circle cx='60' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/></svg>

steps.title: Place
steps.body: Toss a coin to see who starts. Take turns placing one piece on an empty point. Three of yours in a straight line wins at once.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'><rect x='60' y='15' width='80' height='90' fill='none'/><line x1='100' y1='15' x2='100' y2='105'/><line x1='60' y1='60' x2='140' y2='60'/><line x1='60' y1='15' x2='140' y2='105'/><line x1='140' y1='15' x2='60' y2='105'/></g><circle cx='60' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/></svg>

steps.title: Move
steps.body: When all six pieces are down, take turns sliding one of your pieces along a line to an empty point next to it. No jumping.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'><rect x='60' y='15' width='80' height='90' fill='none'/><line x1='100' y1='15' x2='100' y2='105'/><line x1='60' y1='60' x2='140' y2='60'/><line x1='60' y1='15' x2='140' y2='105'/><line x1='140' y1='15' x2='60' y2='105'/></g><circle cx='60' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='15' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='60' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='100' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='140' cy='105' r='5' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/></svg>

steps.title: Win
steps.body: The first to make a straight line of three wins.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g transform='translate(55,55)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#C75B39'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g><g transform='translate(145,55)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#2D3127'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g></svg>

steps.title: Draw
steps.body: If the same position keeps coming back, or after 20 moves each, call it a draw.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g transform='translate(55,55)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#C75B39'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g><g transform='translate(145,55)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#2D3127'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g></svg>

what_to_notice: Did the first piece in the centre matter?
When did you make two threats at once?
How did the game change once pieces started moving?

animation.narration: P1 places in the centre.
P2 places top middle.
P1 places top-left, threatening the diagonal.
P2 blocks at bottom-right.
P1 places bottom-left: two threats at once, the left side and the other diagonal.
P2 can block only one, and places top-right.
All six are down. P1 slides the centre piece left, making three down the left side. P1 wins.

questions.question: What happens after all six pieces are placed?
options: Players slide one piece along a line to an empty point next to it
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look again at step 3.

questions.question: Why could P2 not stop P1?
options: P1 made two threats at once and P2 could block only one
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look at the frame where P1 places bottom-left.

questions.question: How did P1 finish the line?
options: Slid the centre piece to the left side
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Compare the last two frames.

questions.question: If you wanted the first player to have less of an advantage, what would you change?
options: The first piece may not go in the centre
The second player gets four pieces
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Banning the centre removes the strongest opening; an extra piece helps the second player; jumping makes lines harder to hold. Talk about which you would try, and what it would change.

title: Set — three that all match or all differ
parent_game: SET, a card game designed by Marsha J. Falco

credits.by: Marsha J. Falco, 1974; published by Set Enterprises
credits.version: Homemade and without shading: 27 cards instead of 81

lesson: Everyone looks at the same cards at once, with no turns, so perception wins over planning. It shows simultaneous play, and how a single matching rule can carry a whole game.
equipment: 27 paper cards you draw: one for every mix of number (1, 2 or 3), shape (diamond, oval, squiggle) and colour (red, green, purple)
intro: Twelve cards lie face up. Everyone looks at once for three cards where every feature is either the same on all three or different on all three. Whoever sees one first and calls 'Set!' takes it. There are no turns.

steps.title: Make 27 cards
steps.body: Draw one card for every mix of number (1, 2 or 3), shape (diamond, oval, squiggle) and colour (red, green, purple), with every shape filled in. The published game adds a fourth feature, shading, and has 81 cards.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g transform='rotate(-9.0 57 100)'><rect x='40' y='28' width='34' height='50' rx='3' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='57' y='59' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='16' font-weight='600' fill='#2D3127'>◆</text></g><g transform='rotate(-3.0 91 100)'><rect x='74' y='28' width='34' height='50' rx='3' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='91' y='59' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='16' font-weight='600' fill='#2D3127'>●●</text></g><g transform='rotate(3.0 125 100)'><rect x='108' y='28' width='34' height='50' rx='3' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='125' y='59' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='16' font-weight='600' fill='#C75B39'>≈≈≈</text></g></svg>

steps.title: Lay out twelve
steps.body: Shuffle and lay twelve cards face up.

steps.title: Find a set
steps.body: A set is three cards where, for each feature, the three are all the same or all different. Everyone looks at once.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g transform='rotate(-9.0 57 100)'><rect x='40' y='28' width='34' height='50' rx='3' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='57' y='59' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='16' font-weight='600' fill='#2D3127'>●</text></g><g transform='rotate(-3.0 91 100)'><rect x='74' y='28' width='34' height='50' rx='3' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='91' y='59' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='16' font-weight='600' fill='#2D3127'>●●</text></g><g transform='rotate(3.0 125 100)'><rect x='108' y='28' width='34' height='50' rx='3' fill='white' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='125' y='59' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='16' font-weight='600' fill='#C75B39'>●●●</text></g></svg>

steps.title: Call it
steps.body: Say 'Set!' and point to the three cards. If you are right, take them and lay three new cards. If you are wrong, give back one set you hold, or pay another penalty agreed before you start.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g transform='translate(50,65)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#C75B39'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g><rect x='75' y='14' width='115' height='34' rx='17' fill='#FFF8E8' stroke='#D9883D' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='132' y='36' text-anchor='middle' font-family='Fraunces' font-size='13' font-style='italic' fill='#7A4A1F'>Set!</text></svg>

steps.title: End
steps.body: If nobody can find a set, lay out three more cards. When the cards run out and no set is left, whoever has the most sets wins; equal counts are a draw.
steps.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 200 120' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><g transform='translate(30,55)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#C75B39'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#C75B39' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g><g transform='translate(80,55)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#2D3127'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g><g transform='translate(130,55)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#2D3127'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g><g transform='translate(175,55)'><circle cx='0' cy='-15' r='8' fill='#2D3127'/><line x1='0' y1='-7' x2='0' y2='15' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='-12' y1='0' x2='12' y2='0' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='-8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/><line x1='0' y1='15' x2='8' y2='30' stroke='#2D3127' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round'/></g></svg>

what_to_notice: How did you look: card by card, or at the whole table?
Did you learn to check one feature at a time?
How did it feel when someone else kept calling first?

animation.narration: Twelve cards. R, G and P are the colours: red, green, purple. Everyone looks at once.
P2 calls 'Set!': two green ovals, one purple oval, three red ovals. Shape the same; number and colour all different. P2 takes them.
Three new cards fill the gaps.
P1 calls 'Set!': one red diamond, two green diamonds, three purple diamonds. P1 takes them.
P3 calls 'Set!' on one red squiggle, two red squiggles and one green squiggle. Not a set: two are red and one is green. P3 pays the agreed penalty.

questions.question: When are three cards a set?
options: When they match in every feature
When each feature is either the same on all three or different on all three
When they are the same colour
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look again at step 3.

questions.question: Is 'one red squiggle, two red squiggles, one green squiggle' a set?
options: No, because the colours are two of one and one of another
No, because the shapes are all the same
Yes, because the shapes are all the same
questions.feedback_correct: Right. Colour is neither all the same nor all different, and number fails the same way.
questions.feedback_wrong: Check colour on its own: red, red, green.

questions.question: Do players take turns?
options: No: everyone looks at once, and the first to call takes the set
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look again at the introduction.

questions.question: If you wanted a slower player to find sets too, what would you change?
options: Take turns, with a time limit
Give a point for spotting someone's wrong call
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. Turns remove the race but slow everything down; fewer cards make sets rarer; pairs share both the looking and the speed. Talk about which you would try, and what it would change.

title: 3 Quarters — complete the three-quarter circle
parent_game: 3 Quarters, a board game by Prayas Abhinav

credits.by: Prayas Abhinav, 2022, as a warm-up game for students
credits.rules: Rules, board and pieces at github.com/prayasabhinav/games, under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0

lesson: Every piece placed can complete someone else's circle, so each move weighs your gain against what it gives away, under a 20-second clock. It shows interaction through a shared board, and time as pressure.
equipment: the board, printed from https://github.com/prayasabhinav/games/raw/main/3-quarters/3-quarters-board.pdf : 3 columns by 8 rows of squares; play on the red rows with 2 players, add the green rows for 3, and the blue row for 4; the yellow squares double a circle's score

the pieces, printed from https://github.com/prayasabhinav/games/raw/main/3-quarters/3-quarters-pieces.pdf and cut out: for each player, 8 quarter circles, two each of crosshatched (1 point), dotted (2), plain (3) and black (4)
a phone to time each move
intro: '3 Quarters' is a warm up game. One is receptive, when one is perceiving risk. In '3 Quarters' we constantly feel risk. The risk of some move we are making being helpful to other players and contributing to their winning the round is something all players are mindful of.

steps.title: Arrange
steps.body: Arrange one (add, rotate or remove) quadrant at a time to complete a 3/4 circle.

steps.title: A turn
steps.body: In a turn each player gets to arrange (add, rotate or remove) one piece. You can turn as many corners as the dice (d4) shows. If the dice show 4, you have to turn full circle.

steps.title: Remove
steps.body: To remove a quadrant, place a quadrant with the same pattern on it. Take both (without adding the points that both pieces have). A player can remove a piece only three times in a game.

steps.title: Score a circle
steps.body: The player who completes the 3/4 circle removes the pieces from the board and takes as many points as the constituent pieces.

steps.title: Yellow squares
steps.body: If a 3/4 circle has one of its quadrants on a yellow square, the score is doubled.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: The player with 25 points first wins.

steps.title: Keep the board
steps.body: Avoid emptying the board — it will give you a penalty of 10 points.

steps.title: Twenty seconds
steps.body: Each move has to be made in 20 s. Use a mobile to keep time.

what_to_notice: When did a move of yours help another player finish a circle?
How did the 20-second limit change your play?
Was 25 points too quick a target, or about right?

title: All or Nothing — play a slice, win a pizza
parent_game: All or Nothing, a card game by Prayas Abhinav

credits.by: Prayas Abhinav; cards, rules and box made in 2020
credits.rules: Rules and print files at github.com/prayasabhinav/games

lesson: Completing the pizza early scores fewer points, so waiting is rewarded. It shows how one scoring rule can turn a simple arithmetic race into a game of pushing your luck.
equipment: 48 cards: print them from https://github.com/prayasabhinav/games/raw/main/all-or-nothing/print/all-or-nothing-cards.pdf (one card to a page) with the back from https://github.com/prayasabhinav/games/raw/main/all-or-nothing/print/all-or-nothing-card-back.pdf , or write them on paper: green +1 (6 cards), +2 (12), +3 (6); red −1, −2 and −3 (2 each); black ±4, ±5, ±6 and ±7 (4 each); one 'On the house' card and one 'Double order' card
intro: Each player tries to complete a 12-slice pizza by adding or removing slices. In this simple arithmetic game, all age-groups can have quick fun. Adding or subtracting pizza slices feels like the tussle for resources that we face in life. This tussle can be won by individuals who wait and watch — with alertness, foresight and luck. Winning too early, gives less points (as the number of cards in the play space decide the points).

steps.title: Party scene
steps.body: There is a 12-slice pizza on the table. All the players want the entire pizza to themselves. Each player holds 4 cards; the other cards are the deck.

steps.title: A turn
steps.body: Play one card into the centre and pick one card from the deck. Start the game with any green card.

steps.title: The cards
steps.body: Green cards add slices. Red cards remove slices. Black cards add or remove, as you wish; say which while playing.

steps.title: Say the count
steps.body: After playing a card, say the number of pizza slices in the centre: '3 + 2 = 5'. The number of slices cannot be less than 0 or more than 12.

steps.title: Extra hungry cards
steps.body: Double order: the players have to complete 24 slices to win this round. On the house: a coupon for this round; if you complete the pizza, you score double the number of cards in the centre, and if another player completes it, your card is wasted.

steps.title: Win a round
steps.body: Whoever completes the 12 slices wins the round and scores one point for each card in the centre. Shuffle all the cards except those in players' hands, and begin the next round. The game can continue till you are full with pizzas.

steps.title: Two ways to play
steps.body: Simple: hold your 4 cards in your hand, hidden. Challenge: place your 4 cards face up for the other players to see. Knowing everyone's cards means you have to plan ahead to win, but it also means more points.

what_to_notice: When did you hold back from completing the pizza, to let the centre grow?
Did a red card feel like taking a slice from someone?
How did the Challenge way, with cards face up, change your play?

animation.narration: Four players hold 4 cards each. The pizza is empty: 0 slices. The first card has to be green.
P1 plays green +3: '0 + 3 = 3', and draws a card.
P2 plays green +2: '3 + 2 = 5'.
P3 plays a black 4 and adds it: '5 + 4 = 9'.
P4 plays red −2: '9 − 2 = 7'. Nobody gets the pizza yet.
P1 plays a black 5 and adds it: '7 + 5 = 12'. P1 completes the pizza. Five cards are in the centre, so P1 scores 5.

questions.question: What does a red card do?
options: Adds or removes, as you say
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: Look again at step 3.

questions.question: The count is 9 and P4 plays red −2. What do they say?
questions.feedback_correct: Right.
questions.feedback_wrong: A red card takes slices away.

questions.question: How many points did P1 score for completing the pizza?
questions.feedback_correct: Right: one point for each of the five cards in the centre.
questions.feedback_wrong: Count the cards played this round.

questions.question: Winning too early gives fewer points. If you wanted players to wait even longer before completing the pizza, what would you change?
options: Score double for a round longer than ten cards
Let the pizza be 24 slices every round
Make every card in the centre worth two points
questions.feedback_correct: There is no single answer. A bonus for long rounds rewards waiting; a bigger pizza slows every round; passing lets a player wait without changing the count. Talk about which you would try, and what it would change.

title: Eleusis — guess the dealer's secret rule
parent_game: Eleusis, a card game by Robert Abbott

credits.by: Robert Abbott, 1956
credits.version: Close to Eleusis Express, John Golden's short version: 7 cards each, no Prophet, fewest cards wins

lesson: The rules themselves are what you discover. Players learn by testing guesses against right and wrong, which is how a designer learns what a rule does. The Rulemaker also feels the balance: a rule nobody finds is as dull as one everyone finds at once.
equipment: one standard deck of cards (two if more than five play)
paper and a pen for the secret rule
intro: One player writes a secret rule about which card may follow which. Everyone else plays cards and is told only right or wrong. The game is working out the rule from the line of cards that grows on the table.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: One player is the Rulemaker. They write a secret rule that says whether a card may follow the last correct card, using only suit, number or colour: 'play a card of a different colour', 'alternate odd and even'.

steps.title: Deal
steps.body: Deal 7 cards to each other player. The Rulemaker turns one card face up to start the line.

steps.title: Play
steps.body: Going clockwise, each player plays one card next to the last correct card. The Rulemaker says right or wrong. A right card stays in the line; a wrong card goes just below the last right card, and the player draws one card.

steps.title: Guess
steps.body: After a right play, a player may say what they think the rule is. If it is right, discovery is over; if wrong, they draw a card.

steps.title: End
steps.body: The first player to run out of cards ends the round. Fewest cards in hand wins. Then someone else writes a rule.

what_to_notice: Which wrong card taught you the most?
Was the rule too easy, too hard, or about right? What made it so?
As Rulemaker, how did you choose a rule people could find?

title: Mao — the rules nobody will tell you
parent_game: Mao, a card game played in many versions

credits.by: Traditional, with no fixed rules
credits.version: A short form: 5 cards each and two or three secret rules

lesson: Hidden rules turn every penalty into evidence. It shows how players build a model of a game from feedback alone, and how much frustration a design can carry before it stops being fun.
intro: The dealer knows a few extra rules and nobody else does. Break one and you get a penalty card, with only the name of what you broke. You learn the rules by breaking them.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: The dealer chooses two or three secret rules, such as 'say "have a nice day" when you play a 7' or 'an Ace skips the next player', and tells nobody. The only rule anyone may say out loud is this one.

steps.title: Deal
steps.body: Deal 5 cards each and turn one card face up as the start of the pile.

steps.title: Play
steps.body: Going clockwise, play a card that matches the top card by number or suit. If you can't, draw one card.

steps.title: Penalties
steps.body: When someone breaks a rule, secret or not, the dealer gives them one card from the deck and names the rule broken, without explaining it: 'Failure to say "have a nice day"'.

steps.title: Mao
steps.body: Say 'Mao' as you play your last card. The first player to get rid of all their cards wins and becomes the next dealer, and may add one more secret rule.

what_to_notice: When did you work out a secret rule, and what gave it away?
How did it feel to be penalised for a rule you didn't know?
As dealer, which rule caused the most confusion, and why?

title: Nomic — change the rules as you play
parent_game: Nomic, a game by Peter Suber

credits.by: Peter Suber, 1982
credits.version: A short form: three starting rules, a target of 30 points and two turns each, in place of Suber's full Initial Set of 29 rules and 100 points

lesson: Changing the rules is the move. It makes visible what every designer does between playtests, and shows that every rule serves someone more than others.
equipment: paper and pens to write the rules down
intro: In Nomic, a turn is proposing a change to the rules. The group votes, then you roll a die for points. What you are playing at the end may not be the game you started.

steps.title: Start
steps.body: Write the starting rules where everyone can see them: a turn is one proposal, a vote and a die roll; the first to 30 points wins; changes need everyone to agree. Number every rule.

steps.title: Propose
steps.body: On your turn, propose one new rule or one change to a rule, in writing. Give it the next number.

steps.title: Vote
steps.body: Everyone votes. In the first round a change needs everyone; after that, a simple majority.

steps.title: Roll
steps.body: Roll the die and add it to your score.

steps.title: It takes effect
steps.body: An adopted change applies at once. When two rules disagree, the lower number wins, unless a rule says otherwise.

steps.title: End
steps.body: Stop when someone reaches 30 or after everyone has had two turns. The highest score wins; ties are shared.

what_to_notice: Which change made the biggest difference to how the game played?
Did anyone propose a change only to help themselves? How did the vote respond?
What would you change first if you played again?

title: The Mind — play in order, without a word
parent_game: The Mind, a card game by Wolfgang Warsch

credits.by: Wolfgang Warsch, 2018
credits.version: Homemade cards; levels 1 to 4 only, without the published rewards and throwing stars

lesson: With speech removed, the only channel left is timing. Players build a shared rhythm, which shows how a rule that takes something away can make a new kind of play.
equipment: coins or paper bits for lives
intro: Everyone holds numbered cards and the team must play them all onto one pile in rising order. There are no turns, and nobody may speak or signal. You play when you sense it is time.

steps.title: Set up
steps.body: Shuffle the 100 cards. The team has as many lives as there are players.

steps.title: Deal a level
steps.body: In level 1, deal one card to each player; in level 2, two cards each; and so on. Look at your own cards only.

steps.title: Play in silence
steps.body: Anyone may play their lowest card onto the pile at any moment. No talking and no signals. The pile has to rise: every card higher than the one before.

steps.title: Mistakes
steps.body: If someone plays a card while another player still holds a lower one, the team loses a life. Everyone shows and discards their cards lower than the one played, and the level goes on.

steps.title: End
steps.body: Clear level 4 and the team wins. Lose the last life and the team loses.

what_to_notice: How did you decide when to play a 40?
Did the group find a shared sense of time? When did it break?
What happened when someone hesitated?

title: Exquisite Corpse — draw a body nobody planned
parent_game: Exquisite Corpse, a game of the Surrealist artists

credits.by: The Surrealists in Paris, around 1925
credits.version: Three bands (head, body, legs) instead of four

lesson: Concealment makes collaboration surprising. It shows how hiding information between players can produce something nobody could have made alone, and a game with no winner that people still want to play again.
equipment: a sheet of paper and a pen for each player
intro: Each sheet is folded into three. You draw a head, fold it away so only the neck lines show, and pass it on. The next person draws a body without seeing the head. Unfolded, the creatures belong to everyone and no one.

steps.title: Fold
steps.body: Fold each sheet into three equal bands.

steps.title: Head
steps.body: Everyone draws a head in the top band, with two short lines crossing the fold where the neck goes. Fold the head out of sight and pass the sheet left.

steps.title: Body
steps.body: Draw a body joining the neck lines, add lines for the legs, fold it away and pass left again.

steps.title: Legs
steps.body: Draw the legs and feet.

steps.title: Reveal
steps.body: Unfold all the sheets together. There is no winner.

what_to_notice: What did you do with the two lines you were given?
Which creature surprised its makers most?
Would it be better or worse if you could peek?

title: Consequences — a story written blind
parent_game: Consequences, a parlour game

credits.by: Traditional parlour game
credits.version: Seven prompts, the Cambridge sequence

lesson: A fixed sequence of prompts is a story's structure; the players only fill it in. It shows how much of a narrative game comes from its frame rather than its players.
equipment: a sheet of paper and a pen for each player
intro: Everyone writes one line of a story, folds it away and passes it on. Seven lines later, each sheet holds a story none of its writers has read.

steps.title: The prompts
steps.body: Agree the seven prompts: a name, a second name, where they met, what the first said, what the second said, what happened, and what the world said about it.

steps.title: Write and fold
steps.body: Everyone writes an answer to the first prompt at the top of their sheet, folds it over so it can't be seen, and passes the sheet left.

steps.title: Keep going
steps.body: Answer the next prompt on the sheet you are handed, fold and pass, until all seven are done.

steps.title: Read aloud
steps.body: Unfold the sheets and read the stories aloud. There is no winner.

what_to_notice: Which line made a story work, or broke it?
Did the prompts decide the story more than the writers did?
What prompt would you add?

title: Racetrack — drive a car on squared paper
parent_game: Racetrack, a pencil-and-paper racing game

credits.by: Unknown, known by the 1960s; rules published by Martin Gardner in 1973

lesson: One rule about momentum makes every move depend on the last. It shows how a simple physical constraint creates planning, risk and a track that the players draw themselves.
equipment: a pen in a different colour for each player
intro: Each car keeps its speed from one move to the next and can change it by only one square at a time. Taking a bend means braking early. It is the physics of a racing car in a few lines of rule.

steps.title: Draw the track
steps.body: Draw a closed track on squared paper, a few squares wide, with a start line and a finish line.

steps.title: Start
steps.body: Each car starts on a grid point on the start line. Your first move is one square in any direction, or none.

steps.title: Move
steps.body: Each move repeats your last move, across and up, then changes either part by at most one square. Mark the new point and draw the line to it.

steps.title: Crash
steps.body: If your line leaves the track, or ends on another car's point, you are out.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: The first car across the finish line wins. Cars that cross on the same turn share the win.

what_to_notice: When did you have to start braking for a bend?
Did anyone crash by going too fast? Could they have seen it coming?
How would you draw the track to make the race closer?

title: Sprouts — the drawing that ends itself
parent_game: Sprouts, a pencil-and-paper game by John Conway and Michael Paterson

credits.by: John Horton Conway and Michael S. Paterson, Cambridge, 1967

lesson: The board is drawn by the players, and the moves close the board in. It shows how a game can be made of its own map, and how a growing picture can carry the state of a game.
intro: Start with three dots. Each move joins two dots with a curve and adds a new dot on it. Lines may never cross, and no dot may have more than three lines. The drawing grows until nobody can move.

steps.title: Start
steps.body: Draw three dots, spread apart. Toss a coin to see who starts.

steps.title: A move
steps.body: Draw a curve from one dot to another, or from a dot back to itself, then put a new dot somewhere on that curve.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: A curve may not cross itself, another curve or a dot. No dot may have more than three lines touching it; a loop counts as two, and a new dot starts with two.

steps.title: End
steps.body: When a player has no legal move, the game is over. The last player to move wins.

steps.title: Again
steps.body: Play a few games, and then try four starting dots.

what_to_notice: When could you tell how many moves were left?
Did the shape of the drawing trap anyone?
How did the game change with four dots?

title: Hex — connect your two sides
parent_game: Hex, a game by Piet Hein, found again by John Nash

credits.by: Piet Hein, 1942; found again independently by John Nash, 1947–49
credits.version: A 5 by 5 board, with the swap rule

lesson: Every move is both an attack and a defence, because the same chain that connects one player blocks the other. It shows how a geometric fact can rule out draws, and how the swap rule balances first-player advantage.
equipment: paper with a 5 by 5 diamond of hexagons drawn on it
intro: Each player owns two opposite sides of a diamond of hexagons, and tries to join them with a chain of their own colour. One chain always blocks the other, so the game can never be drawn.

steps.title: The board
steps.body: Draw a diamond of hexagons, five along each side. Each player owns a pair of opposite sides.

steps.title: A move
steps.body: Take turns colouring one empty hexagon. A coloured hexagon never changes.

steps.title: The swap
steps.body: After the first move, the second player may take that hexagon as their own instead of moving, so the first player has no reason to start in the strongest place.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: The first to join their two sides with an unbroken chain of their own hexagons wins. Neighbours share an edge.

what_to_notice: Why can nobody draw?
Did you attack or defend more? Is there a difference in Hex?
What did the swap rule do to the first move?

title: Sim — don't make a triangle
parent_game: Sim, a pencil-and-paper game by Gustavus Simmons

credits.by: Gustavus J. Simmons, 1969

lesson: A game about avoiding, not achieving. It shows a misère goal, and a mathematical guarantee: with six dots someone must make a triangle, so the game always ends.
intro: Six dots, every pair joined by a line. Players colour lines in turn, and whoever first makes a triangle of their own colour loses. With six dots, a triangle always comes, so somebody must lose.

steps.title: Draw
steps.body: Draw six dots in a circle and join every pair with a light line: fifteen lines in all.

steps.title: A move
steps.body: Take turns going over one uncoloured line in your colour.

steps.title: Lose
steps.body: If the three lines between any three dots are all your colour, you lose at once. Crossings in the middle are not dots.

steps.title: Again
steps.body: Play several games, taking turns to start.

what_to_notice: When did you run out of safe lines?
Is it better to go first or second?
How does a game where you avoid something feel different from one where you chase it?

title: Chomp — don't eat the poisoned square
parent_game: Chomp, a game by David Gale

credits.by: David Gale, described in 1973

lesson: The first player can always win, yet on most bars nobody knows how. It shows the difference between knowing a strategy exists and finding it, which is often where play lives.
equipment: paper with a rectangle of squares, 5 by 6
intro: A chocolate bar of squares, with the bottom-left square poisoned. Each bite takes a square and everything above and to the right of it. Whoever has to take the poisoned square loses.

steps.title: The bar
steps.body: Draw a rectangle of 5 rows by 6 columns. Mark the bottom-left square as poison.

steps.title: A bite
steps.body: Take turns choosing any remaining square. Cross it out, along with every square above it and to its right.

steps.title: Lose
steps.body: Whoever crosses out the poisoned square loses.

steps.title: Again
steps.body: Play a few times, and try a 2 by 6 bar to look for a pattern.

what_to_notice: Is going first better here? Why?
Did you find a shape you wanted to leave your opponent?
What did the 2 by 6 bar show you?

title: Kayles — knock down one pin or two
parent_game: Kayles, an old skittles game set out by Henry Dudeney

credits.by: Henry Dudeney, 1908, from an older game of skittles

lesson: Each move can break one game into several smaller games. It shows how a position can be a sum of separate parts, a way of thinking that helps in designing any game with independent areas.
equipment: 12 coins or pebbles in a row
intro: A row of pins. On each turn you knock down one pin, or two that stood side by side. Whoever knocks down the last pin wins, and every move can split the row into separate games.

steps.title: Set up
steps.body: Lay 12 coins in a straight row, touching.

steps.title: A move
steps.body: Take away one coin, or two coins that were next to each other in the original row.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: Whoever takes the last coin wins.

steps.title: Again
steps.body: Play a few times. Notice what happens when the row splits into two shorter rows.

what_to_notice: When did splitting the row help you?
Could you see an answer for short rows that helped with long ones?
What does taking from the middle do?

title: Quantum tic-tac-toe — marks in two places at once
parent_game: Quantum tic-tac-toe, by Allan Goff

credits.by: Allan Goff, 2002, made to teach quantum physics

lesson: Each move is uncertain until a later moment decides it, and the decision is handed to the opponent. It shows how a game can be built to teach an idea from science, with delayed effects as its main mechanism.
equipment: paper with a 3 by 3 grid, squares numbered 1 to 9
intro: Each move puts your mark in two squares at once, and only later does it settle in one. When the marks form a loop, the other player chooses how it collapses. Tic-tac-toe becomes a game of decisions you don't control.

steps.title: A move
steps.body: X goes first. On move 1 write X1 small in two different empty squares; on move 2, O writes O2 in two squares; and so on. A square can hold several small marks.

steps.title: Loops
steps.body: Think of each move as a line between its two squares. When a move closes a loop of these lines, the loop must collapse.

steps.title: Collapse
steps.body: The player who did not close the loop picks one move in the loop and chooses which of its two squares it settles in. That fixes the others: each move in the loop, and any move tied to it, settles in its other square. Settled marks are written large and never move.

steps.title: Last square
steps.body: When only one empty square is left, the last move puts both halves in it.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: Three settled marks of yours in a line wins. If both players get a line in the same collapse, the line whose highest move number is lower scores 1 and the other 1/2. A full board with no line is a draw.

what_to_notice: When did you place a mark to force a loop?
How did it feel when the other player chose your collapse?
Did the rules make sense of entanglement for you?

title: Ultimate tic-tac-toe — your move sends them
parent_game: Ultimate tic-tac-toe, a recent variant

credits.by: Unknown; a recent variant of tic-tac-toe

lesson: Each move has two meanings: a mark here and an instruction to the other player. It shows how linking small games turns a solved children's game into one that rewards foresight.
equipment: paper with nine small tic-tac-toe grids, arranged in a large 3 by 3 grid
intro: Nine small games of tic-tac-toe make one large one. Where you play in a small grid decides which small grid your opponent must play in next. Winning a square can mean sending them where they want to go.

steps.title: The board
steps.body: Draw a large 3 by 3 grid with a small 3 by 3 grid inside each of its nine squares.

steps.title: First move
steps.body: X plays anywhere.

steps.title: Where next
steps.body: The square you played in, within its small grid, names the small grid your opponent must play in next. Top-right square sends them to the top-right grid.

steps.title: Small grids
steps.body: Three in a row wins a small grid; it is then closed. A full small grid with no line is also closed. If you are sent to a closed grid, play in any open one.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: Win three small grids in a row on the large grid. If every grid closes without that, it is a draw.

what_to_notice: When did you give away a small grid to control where your opponent went?
Did you plan two moves ahead?
How is this different from playing nine games of tic-tac-toe?

title: Paper soccer — bounce the ball to goal
parent_game: Paper soccer, a pen-and-paper game from Poland

credits.by: Traditional, best known in Poland
credits.version: A 10 by 8 field; a trapped player loses

lesson: Every line drawn changes what can be drawn next, and old moves create new ones through bouncing. It shows how a game's history can live on the board and become its strategy.
intro: A ball moves one step at a time along the lines of a grid, and every line drawn stays. When the ball lands where lines already meet, it bounces and the same player moves again. The pitch fills with the history of the game.

steps.title: The pitch
steps.body: On squared paper mark a field 10 squares long and 8 wide, with a goal two squares wide in the middle of each short side. The ball starts at the centre point.

steps.title: A move
steps.body: Draw a line from the ball to any of the eight points around it, along a square's side or across its diagonal. The ball is now there.

steps.title: Limits
steps.body: No line may be drawn twice, and none may run along the edge of the pitch. The ball leaves the pitch only through a goal.

steps.title: Bounce
steps.body: If the ball lands on a point that already has a line, or on the edge, the same player moves again.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: Get the ball into the other player's goal. An own goal loses. A player who cannot move loses.

what_to_notice: When did you set up a chain of bounces?
How did the old lines change where you could go?
Did the edges help or hurt?

title: Mū Tōrere — the Māori star game
parent_game: Mū Tōrere, a game of the Māori of Aotearoa New Zealand

credits.by: Traditional Māori game

lesson: A board with a single empty point makes every move a question of who gets stuck. It shows how one restriction, the centre rule, can keep a tiny game from being won at once.
equipment: paper with an eight-pointed star and its centre drawn
4 coins of one kind and 4 of another
intro: Eight points round a star and one in the middle. Each player has four pieces and there is only ever one empty point. The game is about not getting stuck.

steps.title: The board
steps.body: Draw eight points in a ring and one in the centre. Join each point to its two neighbours and to the centre.

steps.title: Set up
steps.body: Put one player's four pieces on four points next to each other, and the other's on the other four. The centre is empty.

steps.title: A move
steps.body: Take turns moving one of your pieces along a line into the empty point. No jumping and no capturing.

steps.title: The centre
steps.body: A piece may move into the centre only if it sits next to an opponent's piece on the ring.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: You win when your opponent cannot move. If the same position comes three times, call it a draw.

what_to_notice: Why does the centre rule exist? What happens without it?
How quickly can a game be lost?
What does a board with only one empty space do to play?

title: Aadu Puli Attam — goats against tigers
parent_game: Aadu Puli Attam, a goats-and-tigers game from Tamil Nadu

credits.by: Traditional, Tamil Nadu and South India
credits.version: Tigers win on five captures; some sources say they must take all fifteen

lesson: Two sides with different pieces, different moves and different goals. It shows asymmetric design: balance comes from tuning numbers such as goats needed and capture counts, not from giving both sides the same thing.
equipment: paper with the 23-point board drawn: a triangle from one apex, crossed by four rows
3 tiger pieces and 15 goat pieces (coins or pebbles of two kinds)
intro: Three tigers hunt fifteen goats. Tigers capture by jumping; goats cannot capture at all, but together they can hem the tigers in. The two sides play by different rules for different goals.

steps.title: The board
steps.body: Draw a point at the top. From it draw four lines fanning down. Cross them with four rows: three rows of six points (the two outer points of each row on side lines) and a bottom row of four. That makes 23 points.

steps.title: Set up
steps.body: Put the tigers on the top point and the two points below it nearest the middle. The goats start off the board. Goats move first.

steps.title: Goats place
steps.body: Until all 15 are on, a goat's turn is placing one goat on any empty point.

steps.title: Tigers
steps.body: A tiger moves one point along a line, or jumps along a line over one goat to the empty point just beyond it, taking that goat. One jump per turn.

steps.title: Goats move
steps.body: Once all goats are on, a goat's turn is sliding one goat one point along a line. Goats never jump.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: Tigers win when they have taken 5 goats. Goats win when no tiger can move.

what_to_notice: Which side felt stronger at the start, and at the end?
How did the goats protect each other?
What would change if tigers needed only 3 goats?

title: Moksha Patam — the board that teaches
parent_game: Moksha Patam (Gyan Chaupar), the Indian game behind Snakes and Ladders

credits.by: Traditional, India; the source of Snakes and Ladders
credits.version: A 50-square board you draw; historical boards had 72, 84 or more squares, laid out differently

lesson: A game made entirely of chance that still carries a meaning, because every square is labelled. It shows how a board's words can make players read luck as a lesson, and how rules can make an argument.
equipment: paper with a numbered board of 50 squares, snakes and ladders drawn on it
a coin or pebble for each player
intro: Ladders begin on virtues and snakes on vices. You roll and move, and the board carries you up or down according to what you land on. The dice decide, but the board says why.

steps.title: The board
steps.body: Draw a board of 50 squares in rows of ten, numbered so that the path snakes back and forth from 1 at the bottom to 50 at the top. Draw five ladders and five snakes. At the foot of each ladder write a virtue, such as generosity or patience; at the head of each snake, a vice, such as anger or greed.

steps.title: A turn
steps.body: Roll the die and move that many squares along the path.

steps.title: Up and down
steps.body: Land at the foot of a ladder and climb to its top. Land on a snake's head and slide to its tail.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: You must land exactly on 50; a roll that would take you past it leaves you where you are.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: The first to reach 50 wins.

what_to_notice: Which virtues and vices did you choose, and why there?
Did the words change how it felt to climb or slide?
Is it a game, a lesson, or both?

title: The Royal Game of Ur — race through the shared middle
parent_game: The Royal Game of Ur, from ancient Mesopotamia

credits.by: Ancient Mesopotamia, about 2600 BCE; rules reconstructed by Irving Finkel of the British Museum
credits.version: Four coins in place of the four-sided dice of the original

lesson: A race with a shared middle, where luck decides the distance and you decide which piece to risk. It shows how a few special squares, the rosettes, shape the whole flow of a game.
intro: Two races share one road. Each player's pieces run their own short lane, cross a middle lane where they can knock each other off, and leave by their own lane. Rosette squares give another throw and keep a piece safe.

steps.title: The board
steps.body: Draw three rows of eight squares, then rub out the 5th and 6th squares of the top and bottom rows: 20 squares remain. Mark a rosette on the 1st and 7th squares of the top and bottom rows and on the 4th square of the middle row.

steps.title: The path
steps.body: Each player uses the outer row nearest them. A piece's path is 14 squares: from the 4th square of your row back to its 1st, then the whole middle row from left to right, then your row's 8th and 7th squares. It leaves the board one step after that.

steps.title: Throw
steps.body: Toss four coins. The number of heads is your move; no heads counts as 4.

steps.title: Move
steps.body: Bring in a new piece onto that square of its path (a throw of 3 puts it on the 3rd square), or move one piece that many squares. Two of your pieces can't share a square. If no move is possible, you lose the turn.

steps.title: Rosettes and capture
steps.body: Landing on a rosette gives another throw, and a piece on a rosette can't be taken. Landing on an opponent's piece in the middle row sends it back off the board to start again.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: The first to take all seven pieces off the board, each by an exact throw, wins.

what_to_notice: When did you leave a piece on the shared road on purpose?
How much did the coins decide?
Why might there be a rosette in the middle of the shared row?

title: Senet — the journey across thirty squares
parent_game: Senet, from ancient Egypt

credits.by: Ancient Egypt; rules reconstructed by Timothy Kendall in 1978
credits.version: A short teaching version after Kendall's reconstruction: five pieces each, four coins for the throwing sticks, and two special squares

lesson: A game whose rules were lost and had to be reconstructed from boards and texts. It shows that any set of rules is a choice, and how a path, a few special squares and a swap rule can carry meaning about a journey.
equipment: paper with a board of 3 rows of 10 squares
intro: One of the oldest board games known. Its rules are lost; the version played today is a scholar's reconstruction. Pieces travel a winding path of thirty squares, and late in the game came to stand for the soul's journey after death.

steps.title: The board
steps.body: Draw 3 rows of 10 squares. Number the path 1 to 10 along the top row left to right, 11 to 20 back along the middle row, and 21 to 30 along the bottom row. Mark square 15 as the House of Rebirth and square 27 as the Water.

steps.title: Set up
steps.body: Place the ten pieces on squares 1 to 10, alternating colours.

steps.title: Throw
steps.body: Toss four coins: one, two, three or four heads move that many squares; no heads moves 5.

steps.title: Move
steps.body: Move one of your pieces forward by the throw. You can't land on your own piece. Landing on a lone opposing piece swaps the two. Two of an opponent's pieces side by side protect each other: you can't land on either.

steps.title: The Water
steps.body: A piece that lands on 27 goes back to the House of Rebirth, square 15.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: A piece leaves the board when a throw takes it past 30. The first player to take all five pieces off wins.

what_to_notice: How did the swap rule change where you wanted to land?
Did knowing the board's later meaning change how the Water felt?
Which rules would you change if you were reconstructing it?

title: Kemps — tell your partner without a word
parent_game: Kemps, a partnership card game

credits.by: Traditional

lesson: Information has to cross between partners through a hidden channel, while the other team tries to read it too. It shows how a game can be about communication itself, and how a forbidden channel (speech) pushes play into another.
intro: Partners agree a secret signal before the game. Cards are swapped at speed from the middle of the table, and when one partner holds four of a kind, the other must notice the signal and call it, before the other team spots it too.

steps.title: Signals
steps.body: Each team goes aside and agrees a silent signal meaning 'I have four of a kind': a gesture or a look. No words. False signals to mislead are allowed.

steps.title: Deal
steps.body: Partners sit opposite. Deal four cards to each player and four face up in the middle.

steps.title: Swap
steps.body: There are no turns. Anyone may take a card from the middle and put one of theirs in its place, as often as they like. When nobody wants the middle cards, the dealer clears them and deals four new ones.

steps.title: Kemps
steps.body: If you think your partner has four of a kind, say 'Kemps'. If they do, the other team takes a letter; if not, your team does.

steps.title: Stop Kemps
steps.body: If you think an opponent has four of a kind, say 'Stop Kemps'. If one does, their team takes a letter; if not, yours does.

steps.title: End
steps.body: If the deck runs out with no call, nobody takes a letter. A team that collects K-E-M-P-S loses.

what_to_notice: What signal did your team choose, and did the others read it?
How did watching your partner change how you played your own cards?
Was it harder to collect cards or to read the table?

title: Liar's Dice — bid on dice you can't see
parent_game: Liar's Dice (Dudo, Perudo), a bluffing dice game

credits.by: Traditional; played across South America as Dudo or Perudo
credits.version: Three dice each, paper in place of cups, and no wild ones

lesson: Every bid is a claim you can't check without risking a die. It shows how bluffing works when information is shared but hidden, and how a game tightens as each loss shrinks what you know.
equipment: a sheet of paper each, folded to hide your dice
intro: Everyone rolls in secret. Players take turns raising a bid on how many dice of a face are on the whole table, until someone calls the last bid a lie. Then all dice are shown and someone loses a die.

steps.title: Roll
steps.body: Each player rolls three dice behind a folded paper and looks only at their own.

steps.title: Bid
steps.body: The first player bids a number and a face: 'four 3s', meaning there are at least four 3s among all the dice on the table.

steps.title: Raise or call
steps.body: Going clockwise, each player either raises the bid (more dice, or the same number of a higher face) or calls 'Liar'.

steps.title: Reveal
steps.body: On a call, everyone shows their dice. If there are fewer of that face than the bid, the bidder loses a die; otherwise the caller loses one.

steps.title: Next round
steps.body: Everyone rolls again. The player who lost a die starts the bidding.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: A player with no dice left is out. The last player with dice wins.

what_to_notice: How did you guess what others held from their bids?
When did you bid on something you didn't have?
How did the game change as dice ran out?

title: Cuttle — the first fighting card game
parent_game: Cuttle, a two-player card game

credits.by: Traditional, American; rules as kept by the Cuttle community today
credits.version: The modern rules, as played on cuttle.cards

lesson: A small deck carrying many card powers, each answering another. It shows how a designer gives every card a role, builds counters into the rules, and makes a race into a fight.
intro: Number cards are points; face cards and some numbers do things. You race to 21 points while scrapping your opponent's cards, stealing them and changing the target. Often called the first combat card game, long before trading card games.

steps.title: Deal
steps.body: Deal 6 cards to the dealer and 5 to the other player, who goes first. The rest is the deck. Hold no more than 8 cards.

steps.title: A turn
steps.body: Do one thing: draw a card; play a number card (Ace to 10) to your table as points equal to its number; play it on a smaller point card of your opponent's to scrap both (ties go by suit, clubs lowest, then diamonds, hearts, spades); or play a card for its effect.

steps.title: Royals stay on the table
steps.body: King: you need fewer points (21, then 14, 10, 5 and 0 with one, two, three or four Kings). Queen: your other cards can't be targeted. Jack: take one of your opponent's point cards. Eight played as Glasses: your opponent plays with their hand shown.

steps.title: One-off effects
steps.body: Play a number card to the scrap pile for its effect. Ace: scrap all point cards. Two: cancel an effect just played, or scrap a royal. Three: take any card from the scrap pile. Four: your opponent discards two at random. Five: discard one, then draw three. Six: scrap all royals. Seven: turn up the top two cards and play one. Nine: put one of your opponent's cards on top of the deck.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: Reach your target in points on your table. When the deck is empty you may pass; three passes in a row is a draw.

what_to_notice: Which card changed the game most when it was played?
When did you hold back a Two to answer your opponent?
Which rule would you remove to make it simpler, and what would be lost?

title: Mendikot — win the tens
parent_game: Mendikot, a partnership card game of Gujarat and Maharashtra

credits.by: Traditional, western India
credits.version: Open trump, and a match of first to 3 points

lesson: Trick-taking with a single prize: the tens. It shows how a game can strip a big system down to one thing to fight over, and how partnerships form a silent conversation through the cards played.
intro: A trick-taking game where only the four tens matter. Partners sitting opposite try to capture tens in the tricks they win. Taking all four is a mendikot.

steps.title: Deal
steps.body: Partners sit opposite. Before dealing, show a random card from the shuffled pack: its suit is trump. Put it back, shuffle, and deal all 52 cards, 13 to each player.

steps.title: A trick
steps.body: The player to the dealer's right leads any card; play goes anticlockwise. Each player must play a card of the suit led if they can; if not, any card.

steps.title: Who wins a trick
steps.body: The highest trump wins; if no trump was played, the highest card of the suit led. The winner takes the four cards and leads the next trick.

steps.title: Score the deal
steps.body: After 13 tricks, the team holding three or four tens wins the deal. If the tens split two and two, the team with seven or more tricks wins it.

steps.title: Mendikot
steps.body: Winning all four tens is a mendikot and scores 2 points; any other won deal scores 1. The first team to 3 points wins.

what_to_notice: When did you play a ten, and when did you hold it back?
How did you read what your partner held?
Why might only the tens count?

title: Penney's game — the second chooser wins
parent_game: Penney's game, a coin game by Walter Penney

credits.by: Walter Penney, 1969

lesson: A game that looks fair and isn't. It shows how probability can surprise players, and why designers test balance instead of trusting how a rule looks.
intro: Each player picks a run of three coin tosses, such as heads-heads-tails. A coin is tossed until one of the runs appears. It looks like a fair bet, but whoever picks second can always choose a run that comes first more often.

steps.title: Choose
steps.body: The first player names a run of three, like HHT. The second player, having heard it, names a different run of three.

steps.title: Toss
steps.body: Toss the coin again and again, writing each result in a line.

steps.title: Win
steps.body: Whoever's run appears first in the line, as three tosses in a row, wins the round.

steps.title: The trick
steps.body: The second player can always choose well: take the opposite of the first player's middle toss, then add their first two. Against HHT, choose THH.

steps.title: Play
steps.body: Play ten rounds, swapping who chooses first, and count the wins.

what_to_notice: Did the results look fair or not, before you knew the trick?
Why does the second player have the advantage?
Where else might a fair-looking setup hide an advantage?
